items.title: The Atlanta Dream Can Poke And Prod You To Death
items.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
items.content:
The argument against the Atlanta Dream says their transition-heavy style might be incompatible with playoff basketball. But in the three playoff games they’ve played so far, the latest a 92-82 home win over New York to open the second round, Karl Smesko's team has totally set the terms. As they see it, thisplayoff basketball: fast, tireless, always connected. 

Even when the Dream bump into issues running their halfcourt offense, they make the math work for them in other ways. The best offensive rebounder in league history wins them extra possessions, and a team defense that’s forced more turnovers than any other WNBA team this year sets up easy scoring opportunities against defenses on their heels. That made them a nightmare first-round matchup for the Washington Mystics, who turned the ball over more than any other WNBA team this year. Washington’s season indeed ended thanks to a 42-15 turnover differential across two games.

Lest that stat be blamed on the young Mystics’ nerves, consider the 32 points Atlanta scored off 21 turnovers from veteran-stocked New York in Sunday's game. The fix for Game 2 on Wednesday sounds easy: Don’t turn the ball over. But the Atlanta Dream are a team designed to make it difficult. The Liberty’s problems weren’t all self-inflicted.

items.title: Phoebe Bridgers Showed Us How To See In The Dark
items.author: Kelsey McKinney
items.content:
When the lights went out, a crisp, adolescent shriek rose from all sides of the arena, anticipating her arrival. But she did not come, not just yet. Instead, a silence fell heavy and unsettled where the shrieking had been, as if making space for the ball at the other end of the arena, descending ever so slowly, blinking blue, pulsing as if it were alive. More than 40,000 eyes fixated on the descending orb. It was round, but not a perfect sphere, with bumps and craters on its surface like a morning star weapon with all of its spikes truncated, or a children’s bumble ball powder coated in black. 

Though I was on the other side of the arena, and thousands of people were between me and the ball, it was dark, and there was nothing but air to separate us. I looked at the ball the way I look at the moon: with an awe bordering on reverence. Then it followed the same slow path back up into the rafters, and for a little while, I forgot about it. 

On the main stage a large half-circle dome rested atop the space where Phoebe Bridgers would eventually emerge, like the kind of mesh tents that protect food from the bites of prowling bugs. As the ball on one side of the arena disappeared, the tent on the other lit up. The shrieks began again. And then it lifted, lights gleaming from the edge of it straight down so that Bridgers' black dress was awash in so much light that it looked gray, and the whole dome had the appearance of a UFO lifting off the ground in a movie.

items.title: Patience Is Paying Off For Bryce Young
items.author: Israel Daramola
items.content:
I'm not sure when we fell into the collective delusion that first-round quarterbacks should be capable of leading an NFL team on Day 1. Was it induced by the take economy? Is this sports radio's fault? Did Joe Burrow's early success create this standard? I can understand certain teams like the Browns or Jets believing it necessary to have their top draft pick run the offense right away, because they have little hope otherwise, but what's everyone else's excuse? While you may get Andrew Luck or Lamar Jackson on occasion, often these teams just end up stunting the growth of potential stars, who end up having to rehab their careers and abilities elsewhere.

I was thinking about these things Sunday night while watching Bryce Young have arguably the best game of his career for the Carolina Panthers, against the Detroit Lions. Young led the Panthers to a 32-26 win while throwing for 329 yards and two touchdowns on 29-of-41 passing. Second-year wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan was the biggest beneficiary, accounting for 43 percent of the Panthers' total yardage. He caught 14 passes for 192 yards, and accounted for those two TD passes.

Young and McMillan's chemistry has been building since last season, and never was it more useful than when last night's game was on the line. Despite outplaying the Lions for most of the game, the Panthers were in a spot of trouble late in the fourth quarter. After Detroit scored and cut the lead to six, Young and the offense took over on their own 36-yard line with 3:38 left to play. At the very least, the Panthers needed to get a first down and force a few timeouts out of the Lions. A one-yard run by Chuba Hubbard forced the first burned timeout, and then a penalty followed by an incompletion put Young in a tough spot. Suddenly it was third-and-14, only 22 seconds had come off the clock, and Young was scrambling to avoid pressure. That's when he saw McMillan near the sideline, and made an absurd throw to invite an incredible catch:

items.title: The Case Against Exceptionalism
items.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
items.content:
The first line in a Min Jin Lee novel gives you the whole story. In Free Food For Millionaires, it’s “Competence can be a curse.” In her follow-up, , it’s “History has failed us, but no matter.” Both establish the thesis and themes of the novels, and of her larger project of writing about the Korean diasporic experience. 

The first line of Lee’s latest novel, , does the same: “The rules of engagement have changed already.” The novel, which came out last week nearly a decade after was published, situates her characters—and by extension, the Korean diaspora—at a point of transition where they must adapt. Ever concerned with the financial realities of Korean families, in , Lee considers the cost, both economic and human, of a people striving to elevate itself.

tells the story of a community centered around a hagwon founded in Los Angeles by Korean immigrants. Hagwons are cram schools that are incredibly popular in South Korea, and in the U.S. among Korean communities. They exist to supplement the day-to-day education students get at school. Students often attend them every day after school and late into the night, doing extra work to get ahead academically and to prepare for the highly competitive exams required for admission to the top Korean universities, as well as elite American universities.

items.title: Atlanta’s Least Heralded Relievers Did The Most
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
The Atlanta Braves are not the best team in this postseason, but there do seem to be more of them than anyone else. Manager Walt Weiss has appeared blithely unconcerned by the math that demonstrates that the more pitching changes a team makes, the greater the likelihood that some of them will turn to shit.

And yet Weiss persists, because these are the tools that have been provided for him. After the attrition of the regular season, he has at his disposal three discernible starting pitchers; the best of those, Chris Sale, already had to close out one game against the Phillies in Atlanta's wild-card win, and has not yet started in the team's NLDS. In a more normal environment, this "all hands on deck" strategy would be pointing toward a very predictable outcome: a mutiny by the crew.

But Sunday was the acme of that plan to date. The Braves beat the Dodgers, 3-2, in Game 2 of the National League Division Series, because of stellar work by a 32-year-old ultra-journeyman whose career has been dominated by surgery rehab, and a 21-year-old puppy who fetches whatever is thrown his way because that's what 21-year-olds get to do this time of year. More or less everyone in the Atlanta bullpen was called upon to contribute to the team's most important game of the year so far, and more or less everyone did.

items.title: How Lucy Yu Learned To Ask For Help
items.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
items.content:
Who among us has not floated the idea of starting a bookstore to our friends and partners, as a way out of the nightmare that is 9-to-5 work and LinkedIn hell? In 2021, Lucy Yu actually did it. She had been unhappily working as a chemical engineer and socking away money, and when she had $40,000 saved, she took the plunge and opened Yu & Me Books, the first Asian American woman-owned bookstore in New York City.

Yu & Me Books was the fantasy embodied. It was a cozy space in Chinatown, filled with Yu's favorite books and new releases, and she hosted author and community events each week. But that fantasy was only possible because Lucy was pushing her body and mind to the absolute limit of what she could handle. Everything changed when a fire nearly destroyed her shop in 2023. I've been a fan and supporter of Yu & Me since it first opened, but I was curious to talk with Lucy about how the fire forced her to learn that in order to take care of her community, she had to learn to take care of herself first.

items.title: Jaguars Junction: Week 4
items.author: Hamilton Nolan
items.content:
Are you grasping for an explanation of the Jacksonville Jaguars' typically excellent performance? Look no further than the Microsoft Surface. Microsoft Surface tablets are in the hands of all the Jaguars coaches on the sidelines now, and players are allowed to look at them as well. You can even buy a Jacksonville Jaguars skin to customize your own Microsoft Surface at home. 

With Microsoft Surface, the opposing team can no longer hide behind their helmets. A few clicks or swipes of the virtual keyboard brings up all the information about them that was heretofore concealed. That includes photographs of the faces of each player, their height, weight, and colleges attended. Where past generations of football teams may have focused on developing better footballs or shoulder pads, the Microsoft Surface delivers the Jacksonville Jaguars the most powerful differentiator in the modern NFL: information. 

Data unearthed by Microsoft Surface can be relayed by coaches directly into earpieces in the helmets of each Jacksonville Jaguar. Then a defensive lineman, for example, can look across at the offensive lineman on the other team and say, "Your facemask no longer intimidates me. You are Dalton Risner. You attended Kansas State University. Your favorite food is chocolate. I can tell you the exact address of your parents and other loved ones. A team of assassins is sitting outside of their homes, as we speak. The choice before you now is simple. Either you allow me to run past you, or you will never see them again." Then the Jaguars player could describe in detail what their houses look like on Google Maps. Dalton Risner doesn't know if the other guy is telling the truth, or if the assistant coach just fed him all that information from the sidelines. But does he want to take the chance?

items.title: The Crossword, Oct. 5: Overheard In New York
items.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
items.content:
Our Monday crossword? It's good! This week's puzzle was constructed by and edited by Hoang-Kim Vu Drew is a writer and editor for a national education non-profit who grew up in the Indianapolis area. Although he has lived in the Bay Area since 2013, he hasn’t renounced his Indiana Pacers fandom for the Warriors because his adoration for Reggie Miller’s heroics is so strong. Despite his decades of cheering for Indiana against its fiercest rivals, he couldn’t resist this puzzle’s theme. He hopes Pacers fans forgive him.

Defector crosswords, launched in partnership with our friends at AVCX, run every Monday. If you’re interested in submitting a puzzle to us, you can read our guidelines HERE.

items.title: The Valkyries Are Fighting Firepower With Frenzy
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
Before Sunday's semifinal Game 1 in Ballhalla, the Valkyries threw a little ceremony to honor Janelle Salaün for winning Sixth Player of the Year. Salaün's unanimous approval by voters is one indication of her team's tremendous depth; another, stronger one is that the Valkyries overwhelmed the Aces, 71-60, thanks primarily to their bench and even as Salaün missed both of her shots, scored two points, and played six anonymous minutes.

What makes the Valkyries special? Simply: There are so many of them. Sure, fine, also the defense, though the Valks' defense is in large part a function of their depth. Their bench scores more than anyone else's, and no other playoff team's starters get anywhere near as much rest as Golden State's. Not having to manage around the limits of, say, Breanna Stewart playing 33 minutes per game allows Natalie Nakase's team to operate at a higher intensity for a longer amount of time and mix up the looks they give opponents. However, the unfortunate predicament facing any team structured to play this way is that the playoffs are all about playing Breanna Stewart as much as possible, not having a bunch of overtalented eighth players buzzing around off the bench.

At least in theory. Game 1 showed how devastating Golden State's depth can be. You could see it in the way the Valkyries closed, with Kaitlyn Chen not only stepping in for Veronica Burton but running a form of crunch-time offense built around her repeatedly cooking Mai Yamamoto. You could see it in Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young's combined 9-for-29 night, the product of being hounded for every inch of court by a rotating cast of good athletes. You could see it personified in Aminata Gueye, a backup center the team signed two weeks ago and trusted to play her first non-garbage time minutes in a crucial playoff game against the best player in the league. You could definitely see it in the gaudiest stat of the night: the Valkyries' 17 offensive boards and plus-27 rebounding margin. That was the subject of the first question Nakase fielded in her postgame presser, and she credited the rebounding masterclass to the team's depth.

items.title: Eagles Fans Demonstrate How To Get Humbled By Opposing Coaches
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
I want you to imagine you are a Philadelphia Eagles fan. I know it can be difficult to formulate a theory of mind for them, but if it can be done for a bat, it can be done for a Philadelphian. OK, ready? Go.

You are a Philadelphia Eagles fan. You suddenly have a constant craving for large sandwiches. Your head is now filled with detailed biographical knowledge of several local meteorologists. Every proper noun in this story is familiar. "Pond Lehocky" means something to you. The shouted phrase "FORMAN MILLS" plays randomly in your head at all hours. You are drunk. Drunker than normal, because it is game day. You have probably been tailgating, which is so important to you that you have reinvented collective bargaining from first principles in order to protect your right to drink next to the stadium as opposed to one lot farther out.

You are drunk and feeling good. Your Eagles have been leading since the first drive of the second quarter. They are up 20-10 on the Rams. But not all is well. Jalen Hurts completes just two passes in the second half. They run an unsuccessful Tush Push. They unadvisedly go for it on fourth down with about eight minutes left, and fail, then allow Los Angeles to score touchdowns on two quick drives. The Eagles lose.

items.title: Jackson Chourio Was Nails
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
Mason Miller wasn't looking like himself by the time Jackson Chourio stepped to the plate in the bottom of the ninth of Game 2 of the NLDS. After making quick work of three Brewers hitters in the bottom of the eighth inning, Miller was trusted to go back out there for the ninth and protect the Padres' 3-2 lead. It was only the third time all season he'd been called on to pitch six outs, and by the time he'd recorded two outs in the ninth he'd also issued three walks. The most unhittable pitcher in baseball wasn't getting hit, but he was in trouble nonetheless.

None of this is meant to diminish what Chourio did next. It is only meant to establish that baseball is a game that unfolds as a series of discrete moments that are not necessarily related to what came before. The first three batters Miller faced were blown away, and then three more benefited from the fact that he was having some trouble locating his slider. Chourio watched all of this from the dugout and the on-deck circle, and as he stepped to the plate with two outs and the bases loaded and his team down a run, he had to decide how to attack Miller. Baseball's most indomitable relief pitcher had just given out three free passes, and it's very rare that anything nearly as good as getting on base comes from swinging at one of Miller's pitches. A good time to keep the bat the shoulder, no?

Miller, too, had to make a decision. He could decide to let what had already happened in the inning affect how he approached Chourio's at-bat, or he could put it all out of his mind. He could remember that he's Mason fucking Miller, the guy who struck out 129 batters in 70 regular-season innings and allowed 13 earned runs all year. He could decide that everything that had just happened didn't matter, and all he needed to do to get his team a win was get one out.

items.title: They Packed The Trop And Were Treated To A Gem
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
Bryan Baker, closer for the Tampa Bay Rays, encountered a new problem on the mound Saturday night. He'd been summoned to record the final three outs of Game 1 of the ALDS and to preserve and finish a franchise all-timer of a gem from teammate Drew Rasmussen, who'd pitched eight shutout innings of miraculous one-hit baseball against the New York Yankees' depleted but still fearsome lineup.

Baker, working out pitch-sequencing with catcher Liam Hicks, found that he was having trouble making out the sounds coming from the little PitchCom speaker buzzing right next to his ear. After a 1–1 fastball nicked the outside of the zone against pinch hitter Giancarlo Stanton, Baker had to cup his glove over his ear to hear the call.

"That was probably the most electric crowd I've ever played in front of," Baker said after the game, a 1–0 Rays victory. "Still kind of digesting it."

items.title: Ty France And The Padres Thwarted By Good Old Reality
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
Ty France talks like a guy who is pretty sure he'd socked a game-winning dinger. "I stood there and watched it, and it was going," France said Saturday, of his ninth-inning moonshot. "It was staying fair." The ball did, in fact, stay fair: Soaring down the left field line, France's fly bonked off a roof cable and dropped, well inside fair territory and directly into the glove of Milwaukee's Jackson Chourio, for San Diego's second out of the ninth inning.

France stood in disbelief, peering and pointing at the approximate spot where his heroic moment was thwarted by an impermeable ceiling. The umpires got together, discussed the stadium's ground rules, and came to a pretty quick conclusion: The ball was fair when it bonked, and thus in play when it fell, and Chourio caught it, and France was out. The Padres went on to lose, 3–2. Sorry.

items.title: The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off Lurches Unsteadily Into Cake Week
items.author: Kelsey McKinney
items.content:
The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off, where Kelsey and Chris attempt to complete the technical challenges from the newest season of The Great British Bake Off in their own home kitchens, with the same time parameters as the professional-grade bakers competing on the show.

It's autumn again. The extremely popular and enduring contest show has returned for its 17th season, or series. The format is pretty straightforward: A dozen enthusiastic amateur British bakers are invited to the show's set—a large tent in a field—to participate in three baking challenges. At the end of those challenges, two judges decide who performed the best across the challenges, and name that person Star Baker. They also decide who performed the worst, and that person is eliminated from the competition. Then everyone goes home for the week, before returning for a new set of challenges, and another round of elimination. At the end of each season, one baker is named the winner, and everyone celebrates together, and the vibes are off the charts.

items.title: It’s Time To Separate The Real Teams From The Clowns
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
We're in the middle of bye season now, which means some of your favorites—Texas, UCLA, Duke, Utah and others—are receiving well-deserved weeks off that will allow their fan bases to forget who they hate the most. Well, not forget, really, but maybe forget to mention for at least a few days. No coaches have been fired yet, but now that we're in October, the time is rapidly approaching where a lot of professional Football Men will be given an opportunity to start spending more time with their families. Apologies to those families for what will befall them.

The rest of the week, though, should be about small moves among big teams, as the upward funnel begins to gain suction and the power teams begin to sort themselves out. Margin of victory will start mattering less as simple victory begins to suffice, and the number of undefeated teams will shrink from its current total of 22 (out of 138, roughly 15 percent). The most intriguing of those teams might be North Dakota State, freshly escaped from dispensing ritual thumpings in the Missouri Valley and released into the allegedly more hostile environs of the Mountain West. They may even make a case for a playoff berth, provided the sentient oil stains on the committee deign to notice them. For the moment, they have to worry about Wyoming, as do we all.

items.title: The Too-Small Lynx Will Have To Answer Some Big Questions
items.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
items.content:
As end-of-season Minnesota Lynx press conferences go, this year’s was pretty subdued. There was no “shit was stolen from us,” no missives delivered against Cathy Engelbert. “I don’t have a speech prepared, so everyone can relax,” Napheesa Collier said at the start of her exit interview Thursday afternoon. After an 87-71 loss to the New York Liberty in Game 2 of the first round of the playoffs, the eliminated Lynx are just looking inward. 

The Liberty, set to the play the Atlanta Dream in the second round starting Sunday, became the first No. 8 seed to knock out a No. 1 seed in the first round. “It sucks,” was all Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve had to say about that distinction after the loss Tuesday night. It probably doesn’t deserve more analysis than that. The strength of this particular No. 8 seed is one reason: The Liberty are a veteran, playoff-tested team still led by one of the greatest players of all time. And in a way it did not a few years ago, when three-quarters of a 12-team league made the playoffs, it does also take a little more accomplishment to appear in the WNBA postseason these days. The last time the Liberty were a No. 8 seed, in 2021, they made the playoffs with a 12-20 record. This year, with a 26-18 record, they finished just seven games back of the Lynx, while eight games separated the Liberty and No. 9 Portland.

Beyond unfortunate history, the first-round loss makes for a sooner-than-expected start to what might be the league’s most interesting offseason. The thought on everyone's mind Tuesday night and again at Minnesota's media availability Thursday was something like: Two's a coincidence, three's a trend. Why has the Lynx season ended in heartbreak for three straight years?

items.title: Jack Smith Did Not Conspire Against Donald Trump While Watching Steph Curry Score 60 Points In An Overtime Loss To The Hawks
items.author: David Roth
items.content:
The most salient part of the accusation that Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt lodged against former special prosecutor Jack Smith in a Senate hearing on Tuesday is that it was wrong. It was ecstatically and grandiosely wrong, and obviously wrong in ways that even a rudimentary blog-level fact check would have caught. It was wrong in ways that would only be possible at this particular low ebb in American political and broader executive function—based on unverified and unvetted information given only to Republican senators by the Department of Justice, too hastily put to oafish misuse by well-credentialed chumps of roughly equal laziness and ambition in the pursuit of a spiteful but otherwise opaque end.

In that sense, it is extremely familiar. If it hadn't ended with Schmitt dangling upside down and blustering like the previously undiscovered suburban version of Yosemite Sam after becoming ensnared in his own malfunctioning perjury trap, it might not even have been news at all. In absolute terms, it was as stupid as more or less anything that's happened on the floor of the United States Senate in a century or so, a half-assed 16x-speed gloss on McCarthyism from people who do not really know what that or anything else was, and whose attention spans have left them incapable of parsing even your wordier memes. In relative terms, this is just what our government is like much of the time.

It is not difficult to see what Schmitt was trying to do, and it is extremely easy to see how and why he and his staff of pale and chittering Renfields screwed it up. That failure is grounded in a tragicomic lack of Ball Knowledge, but also in either a more overtly comic inattention to detail, an aversion to even light investigative work, or both. Schmitt et al went through the DOJ's dump of Smith's text messages and believed they had found evidence of him secretly attending an Atlanta Hawks home game against the Golden State Warriors on Feb. 3, 2024. Accusing someone of attending a Hawks game is rude on the merits, but neither libelous nor scandalous in its own right; why Schmitt believed this was newsworthy, let alone a suitably bouncy springboard to soft-launch his own vice presidential ambitions, is something else entirely.

items.title: The Wuppertal Schwebebahn Is Real And It Is My Friend
items.author: Kathryn Xu
items.content:
When my friend in Cologne asked me if I might want to take a day trip, thanks to Cologne's proximity to various other notable cities (Dortmund, Düsseldorf, Bonn, among others), I said that I would like to go to Wuppertal to ride the Schwebebahn. To which they said, "I that's what you were going to say." My brand is strong.

Before my trip to Germany, I declared this desire to ride the Wuppertal Schwebebahn to many of my close friends, and also several strangers. Some people thought it sounded pretty cool. Others said they were happy for me. More than once I was accused of making up words.

Nothing about the glorious feat that is the Wuppertal Schwebebahn is made up. "Schwebebahn" means suspended railway, or literally "floating train," which is an apt way to describe a dangling monorail. It was the design of German engineer Eugen Langen and opened along and above the river Wupper in 1901, connecting several towns that would eventually merge to form the city of Wuppertal, or literally "Wupper valley." Both the early look of the train and its surroundings are captured in footage shot from the front of the Schwebebahn in 1902. Behold, "The Flying Train."

items.title: Igor Shesterkin Caught His White Whale And Scored A Goalie Goal
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
The thing about all goalie goals is that they rock. There are roughly 175 feet and six prideful skaters between the promised land and any netminder bold enough to even attempt to reach it. There have been but 21 goalie goals, scored by 18 different goalies, in the entire history of the NHL. The thing about Thursday night's goalie goal, specifically, is that no goalie since Ron Hextall has ever so clearly wanted it more than Igor Shesterkin.

He is also exceedingly deserving. He is in that classic New York Ranger situation of being one of the league's elite stoppers, trapped on a team that does not seem capable of building a commensurate roster around him. Surely he thinks about how Henrik Lundqvist retired without a Cup. Surely he should get a little treat from time to time, something just for Igor. Often—notably often—that treat-seeking looks like firing a puck down the ice at an empty net.

He does it so often that home crowds start anticipating the attempt as soon as the opposing goalie heads to the bench. He does it so often that Kenny Albert predicted it 10 minutes before it happened last night. And he has comesoclose. “I feel like probably a dozen times I’ve been on the bench thinking, ‘OK, this one goes in,’ and he barely misses,” said Mika Zibanejad. Shesterkin has said he scored one in juniors and has been chasing that high ever since. But he never found paydirt until last night.

items.title: Mr. Monk And The Unfinished Book
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
One of Monk's most Monk-like episodes in all of occurs in Season 2, Episode 7: "Mr. Monk and the Sleeping Suspect." Adrian Monk, Tony Shalhoub's impersonation of Eeyore if the donkey had severe OCD, has taken to visiting Brian Babbage, a comatose man and his prime murder suspect, for an unofficial therapy session. Monk's actual therapist is away on vacation, and the private detective desperately needs someone to talk to. "He's a good listener," Monk tells his bewildered assistant, Sharona Fleming.

Monk sits by Babbage's hospital bed and spills his many woes while doing what he does best: puttering around and noticing things. Monk notices Babbage's watch is a couple minutes fast—an unacceptable misalignment in his world—and as he fixes the watch, he notices a bit of glue stuck to the face. "What were you gluing?" Monk wonders aloud. Suddenly, a distant clatter causes Monk to whirl around and knock over a flowerpot, spilling dirt on the floor. Such disorder, the viewer knows, is unacceptable to Monk, who promptly fetches a vacuum to clean it up. Trusty wet wipe in hand, Monk unplugs a white cord from an outlet to plug in the vacuum and starts sucking up the dirt. The noise of the vacuum is almost loud enough to obscure the fact that Monk has just unplugged Babbage from life support. The man flatlines, but Monk plugs him back in and manages to restart his heart with CPR. Monk has, per his , both wrecked and saved the day. The scene then cuts to a disgruntled outsider, a nurse, who, like many, disapproves of the Monkness of it all.

Monk's improbable theory—that a man who was literally comatose while the murder happened was, in fact, the murderer—turns out to be right, of course. Brian Babbage had mailed bombs to his siblings so that he alone would inherit their late father's riches. The glue was the clue: The smear on Babbage's watch was evidence of how he glued the bombs inside blue mailboxes so that the packages would drop down and ship months later, after the adhesive degraded. And it turns out that Babbage's near-death experience—his second one, really—actually restarted his heart, allowing the police to confirm his guilt and arrest him.

items.title: Blitzing Is More Common Because Formations Are Becoming Tighter
items.author: Arif Hasan
items.content:
I was trying to puzzle out how to plagiarize my new podcast best friend while simultaneously filling in for him for this week’s Jamboroo, and for all my skill in stealing other people’s takes, I couldn’t figure out how to effectively disguise it.

So instead, I’ll build off what Drew wrote last week while referencing research someone else did. I was trying to see why teams are blitzing more this year, even setting aside blitz maven Brian Flores (his Vikings defense is currently blitzing at a mind-boggling 76.9 percent for the season, according to PFF) and former Flores assistant Daronte Jones, now defensive coordinator at Washington (the Commanders are second in blitz rate at 52.1 percent).

In 2026, it turns out that teams that already loved to blitz are the ones blitzing more—median and bottom-fifth percentile blitz rates have not increased by any amount over the last few seasons. But it still invites the question: Why are blitz-happy teams blitzing more?

items.title: Nation Of Bondholders
items.author: Michael Waters
items.content:
It turns out you can trace America’s 2008 financial crash, in a roundabout way, to 18th-century Prussia. The Seven Years’ War left the kingdom in financial shambles: Just to afford the fighting, Prussia’s king, Frederick the Great, had hired private minters to ramp up currency production. So in 1769, Frederick the Great landed on a novel strategy to keep money flowing into his borders. He organized cash-poor nobles into cooperatives, and began offering, to the highest bidders, bonds based on the value of their land. European investors snapped them up, giving Prussia the injection of cash it needed. It was, as the journalist Robin Wigglesworth writes in his new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic History of How Bonds Built the Modern World, possibly the world’s first mortgage bond sale.

is a rollicking look at the development of the bond market, perhaps the least appreciated—but, Wigglesworth convincingly argues, the most important—financial market in the world today. Wigglesworth connects overzealous use of bonds both to the Great Recession and to America’s massive ballooning $40 trillion national debt. Paired with another recent book, David I. Backer’s As Public As Possible: Radical Finance for America’s Public Schools, which chronicles the crushing consequences of the bond market on public schools, a picture emerges of bonds as a little-noticed, and increasingly popular, lever for inequality.

Whether we realize it or not, bonds interlace nearly every facet of our lives. They are basically IOUs that pay out on fixed terms, and that governments and other large institutions issue to raise money. If you have an investment portfolio, it probably contains a slice of bonds sold by the U.S. Treasury. The interest rates of Treasury bondstend to define the entire market: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates on its long-term bonds, as it did recently, your auto lender and your credit card company will probably soon hike their rates, too. But bonds show up in increasingly far-flung corners of the economy, too.Bonds likely fund your local public school or bridge improvement project, and they facilitate the resale of your home mortgage. Summer camps issue bonds to raise money, and so do hospitals and local, state, and national governments. All kinds of consumer debts can be repackaged as bonds, and sold to ever more distant bidders.

items.title: Mike Tomlin’s ‘Minecraft’ City Is A Delight
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content: When former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin revealed that he had been working on a city for 12 years, I brushed it off. The idea of an NFL coach—a Super Bowl-winning coach who never had a losing season—taking time over a decade-plus to truly lock into city planning just didn't seem realistic, or like the result would be particularly interesting. I doubted Tomlin's gamer credentials.
